analysis.one_liner: Taxes household fortunes above roughly $190 million at annual rates of 2 to 8 percent.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a vote: it was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee on the day it was introduced and sat there until the 118th Congress ended, with 22 Democratic cosponsors and none from the other party.
analysis.plain_summary: The Oligarch Act would create an annual federal wealth tax. Each year, every individual and most trusts would owe a percentage of their net worth above a floor set at 1,000 times the nation's median household wealth — with today's median wealth of roughly $190,000, that floor works out to about $190 million, a level very few households reach. Rates climb from 2% to 8% as fortunes grow, trusts above the threshold pay a flat 8%, the IRS would have to audit at least 30% of those who owe the tax every year, and anyone who underreports asset values faces penalties up to 50%. The bill was introduced by Rep. Barbara Lee in July 2023 and referred to the Ways and Means Committee, which never acted on it.
analysis.who_benefits: Essentially every household in America below the roughly $190 million net-worth threshold pays nothing — the bill's threshold is tied to median household wealth, so it only touches the richest sliver and rises automatically as typical families' wealth grows. If the revenue were used for public programs, the broader public would benefit, though the bill does not earmark the money for any specific purpose.

how_it_helps.text: The tax applies only to net worth above a threshold set at 1,000 times the greater of $50,000 or the nation's median household wealth, so ordinary households are excluded by design.
Rates are graduated: 2% on wealth up to ten times the threshold, 4% up to one hundred times, 6% up to one thousand times, and 8% beyond that, with trusts above the threshold taxed at a flat 8%.

Married couples are treated as a single taxpayer, gifts to children under 18 are counted against the giver to prevent shifting wealth out of the tax, grantor-trust assets are attributed to the grantor, and trusts benefiting substantially the same beneficiaries are combined into one taxpayer.

The IRS must annually audit at least 30% of taxpayers who owe the wealth tax, must report within a year on the assets the tax would cover, and can require financial institutions and businesses to report asset values, including estimates of the value of the businesses themselves.
Penalties are stiffened for undervaluing assets: 30% for substantial wealth-tax valuation understatements and 50% for gross misstatements, and the wealth tax is not deductible from income taxes.

Taxpayers with severe liquidity constraints or ongoing businesses that would face hardship may get up to five years to pay, and the tax does not hit retirement trusts exempt under section 401(a), such as 401(k) plans.

analysis.who_pays: Individuals and trusts with net worth above roughly $190 million — a few thousand households at most — would pay an annual tax of 2% to 8% on the excess, on top of existing income and estate taxes, with no offsetting income-tax deduction. Family businesses and illiquid assets are included in the base, though payment can be deferred up to five years in hardship cases.

drawbacks.text: The bill's math is aggressive by international standards: rates up to 8% of total wealth each year are far above the 1-2% wealth taxes that countries like Spain, Switzerland, and Norway have used, and most European countries that adopted broader wealth taxes repealed them after administrative difficulty and wealthy taxpayers relocating. Those outcomes are widely reported; the bill's own design features — taxing all property wherever situated and delegating formulaic valuation of hard-to-price private assets to the Treasury — are in the text.

Valuing privately held businesses, art, and other assets without market prices is genuinely difficult, which is why the bill authorizes new formulaic valuation methods and financial-institution reporting; opponents would argue this creates a heavy compliance and enforcement apparatus targeted at a small group, and questions have been raised in broader policy debate about whether a federal wealth tax is constitutional without apportionment among the states (a general-policy point not resolved in the bill text).
The bill does not say what the revenue would fund, so its practical benefit to ordinary families depends entirely on choices Congress would make later.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is designed so that well over 99% of households pay nothing and the entire burden falls on multi-hundred-million-dollar fortunes, which is a straightforward trade for most Americans if the revenue is put to public use. The honest objections are about execution, not fairness to typical families: an 8% annual rate on total wealth is far beyond what any country has sustained, valuing private assets invites years of disputes, the constitutionality of a federal wealth tax has been seriously contested, and the bill leaves the use of the revenue undefined. A more modest version would have been far more durable.

outcome.mechanism: It went to the Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced and never came out — no hearing, no markup, no vote, no floor action before the 118th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Barbara Lee of California introduced the Oligarch Act of 2023 in the House on July 26, 2023, with ten original cosponsors.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day, the committee with jurisdiction over tax legislation.
Twenty-two House Democrats cosponsored the bill in total; no Republican did.

The action history shows no further steps — no hearing, no committee vote, no floor action — before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, which means the bill died and would have to be reintroduced from scratch.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Households with net worth above roughly $190 million are better off because the bill died: their fortunes remain untaxed annually and unrealized gains continue to go untaxed until sold. The Ways and Means chair and the Republican majority also avoided having to take a recorded vote on a wealth tax, and the 22 cosponsors kept their support on record at no procedural cost.

for.name: Rep. Barbara Lee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Oligarch Act of 2023, establishing an annual federal wealth tax with graduated rates up to 8% on fortunes above roughly $190 million.

for.name: Reps. Summer Lee, Rashida Tlaib, Jamaal Bowman, Jesús 'Chuy' García, Raúl Grijalva, Jerrold Nadler, Ilhan Omar, Jared Huffman, Bonnie Watson Coleman, and Jamie Raskin
for.what_they_did: Signed on as original cosponsors at introduction; 12 more House Democrats joined later, bringing total cosponsorship to 22.

against.name: Rep. Jason Smith
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: The committee to which the bill was referred took no action on it for the rest of the 118th Congress — no markup or vote was ever scheduled, so the bill never reached the House floor.

against.name: House Republican majority
against.what_they_did: No House Republican cosponsored the bill, and with the Republican majority controlling the committee and floor calendar, no path to a vote existed.

sides.party_line_note: All 22 cosponsors were Democrats and none were Republicans; with a Republican chair and majority controlling the Ways and Means Committee and the House calendar, the bill never advanced.

industries.industry: Ultra-high-net-worth households and their family trusts
industries.note: Households and trusts with net worth above roughly $190 million would owe 2% to 8% of the excess every year, on top of existing income and estate taxes, with anti-avoidance rules aimed at trusts and gifts to young children. Their interest in stopping the bill ran directly against the interest of the vast majority of households the bill would never touch.

industries.industry: Wealth management, trusts and estates, and private financial institutions
industries.note: The bill would require financial institutions and business entities to report detailed asset and entity-value information for wealth-tax enforcement, and grantor-trust attribution would unwind a core service of trust-based estate planning for large fortunes. Compliance would be costly, though the bill also creates work in valuation and advisory services for the few thousand households affected.
